source.title: Syntax vs. Semantics: How Transformers Learn Deep Dependencies

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses different tasks and measures from the original grokking studies, but directly measures training-time semantic alignment, gradient dynamics, and dependency-circuit emergence.
record.gate_note: The paper reports other results, including model comparisons, fine-tuning benchmarks, curvature and representation analyses, and head ablations. These are not recorded as rows unless they measure the training-time circuit emergence or progress dynamics named by V2. The synthetic-task accuracy results do not state a train/test split or training-set-size sweep.
record.test_reason: The study interprets grokking as the alignment ratio ρ(t) crossing a stability threshold, but never measures grokking itself. No condition shows training accuracy saturating while held-out accuracy stays at chance and later jumps. The toy results are training-loss plateaus, a gradient-norm surge, attention crossover, and validation-accuracy curves capped near 0.35. The Pythia results are an alignment metric and attention snapshots with no performance jump. There is no memorization phase, no removal of memorizing components, and no progress measure shown to anticipate a generalization jump. So the rows track sudden emergence of dependency learning, a related but different construct from delayed generalization beyond overfitting.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that high-curvature syntactic gradients starve sparse semantic-dependency gradients early in training, so deep-dependency learning appears as a sharp phase transition tied to the alignment ratio ρ(t). They argue that syntax suppression, CoT supervision and a topology-aligned contrastive objective ease this barrier. They interpret grokking as ρ(t) crossing τstable, but they assert rather than measure the link to delayed generalization.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses synthetic code and dependency probes, gradient/attention analyses, and interventions; it does not reproduce the original modular-arithmetic grokking setup or its train/test-accuracy and dataset-size measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: In the toy interventions, suppressing syntax or removing syntactic markers is reported to accelerate emergence, while noise in variable-token gradients delays it. The reported dynamics also differ between natural-language and code probes.

fits_no_version.finding: In toy transformers on synthetic code, training loss plateaus, then variable-token gradients surge and loss drops sharply. The authors label this 'grokking' of binding (Fig. 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sudden emergence of dependency-binding during training is preceded by suppressed semantic-token gradients (gradient starvation), with no train/test generalization gap.

fits_no_version.finding: Masking syntactic-token gradients or removing syntax markers speeds exit from the early validation plateau. Noising variable-token gradients delays it (single seed).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The timing of an abrupt capability transition can be shifted by manipulating the gradient competition between frequent and sparse tokens.

fits_no_version.finding: In Pythia-160m pretraining, a QK-gradient/operator alignment ratio is ~0, spikes transiently at 5k, and rises monotonically from 20k. Pointer attention in Pythia-1.4B is stable for natural language and delayed for code.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Internal alignment measures of dependency circuits evolve non-monotonically during LLM pretraining.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026 (as stated in the text)
record.problems: The paper gives no uncertainty estimates for these results. The toy experiments use a fixed seed (42), and the text does not state a train/test split for the synthetic task-accuracy curves. Several dynamics are presented qualitatively or in plots; the text gives no numerical accuracy values for those curves. The paper's alignment-ratio definitions differ between the main text and Appendix B.2.
record.rows_left_out: Other reported analyses and benchmark results were left out because they do not measure the temporal circuit-formation or progress dynamics in V2: curvature perturbations, rank analysis, gradient coherence across layers, binding-subspace visualization, head ablation, and fine-tuning benchmark scores (Appendix A, Table 1, Table 2, and Table 3).

untested.parts: No train vs test accuracy curves and no training-set-size sweep. Algorithmic tasks are used, but there is no delayed generalization after saturation.
No memorization phase or removal of memorizing components. No progress measure shown to anticipate a held-out generalization jump.
No delayed generalization on non-algorithmic data. No initialization-scale or weight-norm manipulation.
Pythia checkpoints are probed, but no delayed generalization relative to training performance is reported.
No weight-decay or low-norm efficiency test, critical dataset size, or ungrokking.
Single seed (42). No cross-run algorithm comparison.

record.verdict_notes: Grokking is invoked only interpretively (Sec 2.5, Fig. 2 title). The original sources are only cited. All toy runs use seed 42 with no uncertainty reported. The ρ(t) definition is inconsistent between the main text (gradient-based, squared cosine) and Appendix B.2 (weight-based cosine). The Sec 3.3 natural-language entity-binding replication is mentioned without data. Fine-tuning tables are method comparisons and correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: No stated train/test accuracy curves showing chance test accuracy after training accuracy saturation, and no training-set-size comparison.

The study tracks alignment, gradients, attention, and dependency resolution, but does not measure removal of memorizing components or show that a continuous progress measure predicts a held-out-accuracy jump.
No grokking-like delay sweep on non-algorithmic data and no initialization-scale or weight-norm manipulation.
Pythia checkpoints are analyzed with dependency probes, but the study does not report delayed generalization on realistic pretraining or fine-tuning data.
No low-norm efficiency account, critical dataset size, or ungrokking test.
No comparison of algorithms learned across independent runs of the same task.
No optimizer-instability or floating-point artifact control.

rows.subject: NanoTransformer
rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch; Experiment 1, up to 5000 steps
rows.operation_detail: Tracked average embedding-gradient norms for syntax and variable-token groups during training.
rows.measure: Variable-token gradient norm relative to syntactic-token gradients
rows.value: Variable-token gradients are described as suppressed and comparable to the syntactic baseline early; a later sharp surge is reported.
rows.note: The paper describes the curve qualitatively; no numerical gradient values are stated in the text.
rows.check: Embedding-gradient norms during a training-loss plateau. There is no train/test gap, so this is not grokking. The gradient surge coincides with the loss drop rather than anticipating a held-out jump.

relation.reason: Section 2.5 interprets grokking as an alignment-threshold crossing, but the experiments neither measure grokking nor use an established grokking result as a tool.

tranche.reason: The study measures dependency learning, training-loss plateaus and mechanistic proxies, without establishing delayed held-out generalization after training accuracy saturates. Its theoretical interpretation of grokking does not test a listed claim version.

source_check.notes: The alignment metric is internally inconsistent: Sections 2.5/4.1 use squared gradient alignment, whereas Appendix B.2 Equation 10 uses unsquared weight-matrix alignment. The syntax-free condition appears in Section 3.3 and Figure 4's legend but is omitted from its caption and Appendix B.1's intervention list.
